America imports a lot of products we can make here at home, with some of them crossing oceans several times before arriving in our stores. How can that possibly be efficient?

This explosion of international trade has made the country much wealthier. By driving down prices, expanded trade has saved the average American household over $18,000, with those benefits disproportionately going to the lowest-income families.

But how does sending money to other countries make us wealthier?

113101980870654.ad_body:
Ayo Olopon Game board

Ayo Olopon or Awele is an ancient traditional board game of the Yoruba ethnic group in Nigeria distinguished by its standardized rules and processes. Considered as one of the oldest African board games, there are different variations across different countries in Africa. It is believed to be as old as the Ifa spiritual system. Ayo means seed, while opon refers to the holder or tray. The fusion; Ayo Opon means “seeds in the holder.” 

Ayo gameboards range from everyday objects with simple forms to intricately carved, ornate pieces that serve as a status symbol. Figurative carvings on Ayo gameboards are quite rare and show the creativity Africans put into functional objects.

I owned two houses.
But since I was seventeen, I HADN'T spent a single night in either of them.
The reason? I just couldn't go back.
Because living there instead, my mother, my stepfather.
And the two kids he brought into the mix.
My mom used to say: "We're family, honey. We'll just squeeze in and make it work."
But turned out? I was the one who got squeezed out.
When the relatives found out, they just gave me that look and tried to talk me down: 
"Your mom's had it rough, kid. Just be the bigger person."
The bigger person.
I'd been hearing that nonsense for six years.
Six years later, I finally graduated.
The first thing I did? Wasn't hunt for a job.
I called a locksmith.
Huh. Time to pack up, dear Mom!

The locksmith finished up with the last deadbolt and handed me three shiny new keys.

1003199872885383.ad_body:
I owned two houses.
But since I was seventeen, I HADN'T spent a single night in either of them.
The reason? I just couldn't go back.
Because living there instead, my mother, my stepfather.
And the two kids he brought into the mix.
My mom used to say: "We're family, honey. We'll just squeeze in and make it work."
But turned out? I was the one who got squeezed out.
When the relatives found out, they just gave me that look and tried to talk me down: 
"Your mom's had it rough, kid. Just be the bigger person."
The bigger person.
I'd been hearing that nonsense for six years.
Six years later, I finally graduated.
The first thing I did? Wasn't hunt for a job.
I called a locksmith.
Huh. Time to pack up, dear Mom!

The locksmith finished up with the last deadbolt and handed me three shiny new keys.

"Alright! Anyone who's been a homewrecker—DRINK UP!"
Truth or dare. Someone shoves a drink forward.
Nobody moves.
Then Finn's "girl bro" Nora slides a glass toward ME. Grinning.
"Actually, Finn and I got married a year ago. So technically? You're the homewrecker."
My hands shake. I look at him.
Waiting for him to say something. Anything.
Finn just shrugs.
"Lost a dare. We went and signed papers. Figured we'd undo it someday."
"Then her parents were on her case about marriage, so I just... stayed married. Easier that way."
"But babe, relax. Nora and I are just bros. YOU'RE the one I love."
Amazing.

1159879563874957.ad_body:
Pregnant with my husband's baby—flew to his city to surprise him for our anniversary.
His call hits me at the door: "Babe! Happy five years! Got a surprise for you—arrives tomorrow."
I cover the camera, grinning. 
"I've got a surprise for you too. Five minutes."
Hang up.
This blonde in the elevator smiles at me. 
"Wait—you're Nathan's wife? He talks about you constantly."
My heart melts.
Elevator opens. His office—right there.
Hand on the door.
She grabs me, smile like ice.
"I'm Chloe. Nathan's girlfriend."
"This is our time. Stay here. I'll get you when we're done."
Oh. Guess this is my surprise.

Door slams shut.

I'm frozen. Brain screaming.

Chairs scraping. Then—those sounds.

"Babe, I'm still bruised from last time. Go easy on me?"

No. I didn't hear that.

His voice—unmistakable.

"
